claim: When an action potential arrives at a synapse there is a large probability that no neurotransmitter is released.
source: When an action potential arrives at a synapse there is a large probability that no neurotransmitter is released.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about synaptic transmission and is cited in the manuscript.

claim: Simple computational models suggest that synaptic failures enable information processing at lower metabolic costs.
source: Surprisingly, simple computational models suggest that these synaptic failures enable information processing at lower metabolic costs.
evidence: This refers to previous computational modeling work, as indicated by the context and citations in the introduction.

claim: Presynaptic stochasticity and plasticity improve energy efficiency.
source: We find that presynaptic stochasticity and plasticity improve energy efficiency and show that the network allocates most energy to a sparse subset of important synapses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The network allocates most energy to a sparse subset of important synapses.
source: We find that presynaptic stochasticity and plasticity improve energy efficiency and show that the network allocates most energy to a sparse subset of important synapses.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Stabilising important synapses helps to alleviate the stability-plasticity dilemma.
source: We demonstrate that stabilising these synapses helps to alleviate the stability-plasticity dilemma, thus connecting a presynaptic notion of importance to a computational role in lifelong learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Synaptic signal transmission is stochastic.
source: It has long been known that synaptic signal transmission is stochastic (del Castillo and Katz, 1954).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to del Castillo and Katz, 1954.

claim: When an action potential arrives at the presynapse, there is a high probability that no neurotransmitter is released.
source: When an action potential arrives at the presynapse, there is a high probability that no neurotransmitter is released – a phenomenon observed across species and brain regions (Branco and Staras, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Branco and Staras, 2009.

claim: Large amounts of noise hinder reliable and efficient computation.
source: Large amounts of noise hinder reliable and efficient computation (Shannon, 1948; Faisal et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shannon, 1948 and Faisal et al., 2005.

claim: The brain, and specifically action potential propagation consume a disproportionately large fraction of energy.
source: The brain, and specifically action potential propagation consume a disproportionately large fraction of energy (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Harris et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Harris et al., 2012.

claim: Individual synapses do not merely maximise information transmission, but rather take into account metabolic costs, maximising the information transmitted per unit of energy.
source: One important line of work proposes that individual synapses do not merely maximise information transmission, but rather take into account metabolic costs, maximising the information transmitted per unit of energy (Levy and Baxter, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levy and Baxter, 1996.

claim: The information-per-energy approach has proven fruitful to explain synaptic failures.
source: This approach has proven fruitful to explain synaptic failures (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levy and Baxter, 2002 and Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The information-per-energy approach has proven fruitful to explain low average firing rates.
source: This approach has proven fruitful to explain synaptic failures (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012), low average firing rates (Levy and Baxter, 1996)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levy and Baxter, 1996.

claim: The information-per-energy approach has proven fruitful to explain excitation-inhibition balance.
source: This approach has proven fruitful to explain synaptic failures (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012), low average firing rates (Levy and Baxter, 1996) as well as excitation-inhibition balance (Sengupta et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2013.

claim: Presynaptic glutamate release is tuned to maximise information transmission per energy.
source: is supported by fascinating experimental evidence suggesting that both presynaptic glutamate release (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and postsynaptic channel properties (Harris et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2019) are tuned to maximise information transmission per energy.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Savtchenko et al., 2013.

claim: Postsynaptic channel properties are tuned to maximise information transmission per energy.
source: is supported by fascinating experimental evidence suggesting that both presynaptic glutamate release (Savtchenko et al., 2013) and postsynaptic channel properties (Harris et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2019) are tuned to maximise information transmission per energy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2015 and Harris et al., 2019.

claim: Information-theoretic approaches have been limited to signal transmission at single synapses, ignoring the context and goals in which the larger network operates.
source: However, so far information-theoretic approaches have been limited to signal transmission at single synapses, ignoring the context and goals in which the larger network operates.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous work based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Presynaptic stochasticity in combination with presynaptic plasticity allows networks to extract information at lower metabolic cost by sparsely allocating energy to synapses that are important for processing the given stimulus.
source: We find that presynaptic stochasticity in combination with presynaptic plasticity allows networks to extract information at lower metabolic cost by sparsely allocating energy to synapses that are important for processing the given stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Presynaptic release probabilities encode synaptic importance.
source: As a result, presynaptic release probabilities encode synaptic importance.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2 and theoretical analysis.

claim: The notion of synaptic importance encoded in release probabilities is related to the Fisher information.
source: We show that this notion of importance is related to the Fisher information, a theoretical measure for the network's sensitivity to synaptic changes.
evidence: This is supported by theoretical analysis and data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Selectively stabilising important synapses improves lifelong learning.
source: In line with experimental evidence (Yang et al., 2009; Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015), we demonstrate that selectively stabilising important synapses improves lifelong learning.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5, and is consistent with cited experimental evidence.

claim: Presynaptically induced sparsity is linked to improved memory.
source: Furthermore, these experiments link presynaptically induced sparsity to improved memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the lifelong learning experiments.

claim: The probability of synaptic failures is substantial.
source: The probability of such failures is substantial (Branco and Staras, 2009; Hardingham et al., 2010; Sakamoto et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Branco and Staras, 2009; Hardingham et al., 2010; and Sakamoto et al., 2018.

claim: Artificial neural networks match several aspects of biological neuronal networks in various goal-driven situations.
source: As a growing body of literature suggests, artificial neural networks (ANNs) match several aspects of biological neuronal networks in various goal-driven situations (Kriegeskorte, 2015; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Kell et al., 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Cueva and Wei, 2018; Mattar and Daw, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Artificial neural networks are the only known model to solve complex vision and reinforcement learning tasks comparably well as humans.
source: Crucially, they are the only known model to solve complex vision and reinforcement learning tasks comparably well as humans.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: Synaptic transmission is classically described as a binomial process.
source: Although synaptic transmission is classically described as a binomial process (del Castillo and Katz, 1954)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to del Castillo and Katz, 1954.

claim: Most previous modelling studies assume the synaptic strengths to be deterministic.
source: Although synaptic transmission is classically described as a binomial process (del Castillo and Katz, 1954) most previous modelling studies assume the synaptic strengths to be deterministic.
evidence: This is based on the authors' review of previous modeling literature.

claim: The model with plastic, stochastic release finds considerably more energy-efficient solutions than both deterministic synapses and stochastic synapses with fixed release probability.
source: Figure 1a shows that different magnitudes of ℓ2-regularisation induce different information-energy trade-offs for all models, and that the model with plastic, stochastic release finds considerably more energy-efficient solutions than both controls
evidence: This is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The model with non-plastic release requires more energy than the deterministic model.
source: while the model with non-plastic release requires more energy then the deterministic model.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A combination of presynaptic stochasticity and plasticity promotes energy-efficient information extraction.
source: Together, this supports the view that a combination of presynaptic stochasticity and plasticity promotes energy-efficient information extraction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: After learning, there are few synapses with high release probabilities, while most release probabilities are kept low.
source: Figure 2a shows that after learning, there are indeed few synapses with high release probabilities, while most release probabilities are kept low.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The sparsity in release probabilities develops independently of the initial value of release probabilities before learning.
source: We confirm that this sparsity develops independently of the initial value of release probabilities before learning, see Appendix 1—figure 1d.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1d.

claim: Maintaining synapses with high release probabilities is significantly more important to network function than maintaining random ones.
source: We find that maintaining synapses with high release probabilities is significantly more important to network function than maintaining random ones.
evidence: This is supported by the lesion experiment data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Synapses with high release probabilities consume considerably more energy than synapses with low release probability.
source: Moreover, we find, as expected, that synapses with high release probabilities consume considerably more energy than synapses with low release probability, see Figure 2c.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The model identifies important synapses for the task at hand and spends more energy on these synapses while saving energy on irrelevant ones.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the model identifies important synapses for the task at hand and spends more energy on these synapses while saving energy on irrelevant ones.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figures 2b and 2c.

claim: The distribution of important synapses per neuron is inhomogeneous and significantly different from a randomly shuffled baseline with a uniform distribution of active synapses.
source: We find that the distribution of important synapses per neuron is inhomogeneous and significantly different from a randomly shuffled baseline with a uniform distribution of active synapses (Kolmogorov-Smirnoff test, D=0.505,p<0.01), see Figure 3a.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Some neurons have disproportionately many important inputs, while others have very few, suggesting sparsity on a neuronal level.
source: Thus, some neurons have disproportionately many important inputs, while others have very few, suggesting sparsity on a neuronal level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The model network with presynaptic stochasticity has disproportionate numbers of highly important and unimportant neurons.
source: We find that our model network with presynaptic stochasticity has disproportionate numbers of highly important and unimportant neurons, see Figure 3b.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Neurons with many important inputs tend to have many important outputs, with a correlation of r=0.93.
source: Moreover, we check whether neurons with many important inputs tend to have many important outputs, indeed finding a correlation of r=0.93, see Figure 3c.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The network is sparse not only on a synaptic but also on a neuronal level.
source: These analyses all support the claim that the network is sparse not only on a synaptic but also on a neuronal level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analyses presented in Figure 3.

claim: Release probabilities are more likely to increase for synapses with large Fisher information.
source: Under mild assumptions, we show (Materials and methods) that release probabilities are more likely to increase for synapses with large Fisher information
evidence: This is supported by theoretical analysis presented in Materials and methods.

claim: Synapses with large release probabilities will tend to have high Fisher information.
source: Thus, synapses with large release probabilities will tend to have high Fisher information. We validate this theoretical prediction empirically, see Figure 2d.
evidence: This is supported by theoretical analysis and empirical validation shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Preserving memories requires maintaining the synapses which encode these memories.
source: it has been demonstrated experimentally that preserving memories requires maintaining the synapses which encode these memories (Yang et al., 2009; Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015; Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The Fisher information is a useful way to quantify which synapses should be maintained.
source: In this context, theoretical work suggests that the Fisher information is a useful way to quantify which synapses should be maintained (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kirkpatrick et al., 2017.

claim: The synaptic importance encoded in release probabilities can be used to improve the network's memory retention by selectively stabilising important synapses.
source: Inspired by these insights, we hypothesise that the synaptic importance encoded in release probabilities can be used to improve the network's memory retention by selectively stabilising important synapses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is then tested in the experiments.

claim: The presynaptic consolidation model performs better than a standard model with deterministic synapses and without consolidation.
source: We find that the presynaptic consolidation model performs better than a standard model with deterministic synapses and without consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The presynaptic consolidation mechanism performs better than Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC).
source: The presynaptic consolidation mechanism performs better than both these state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms, see Figure 4c.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The presynaptic consolidation mechanism performs better than Bayesian Gradient Descent (BGD).
source: The presynaptic consolidation mechanism performs better than both these state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms, see Figure 4c.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Removing the consolidation mechanisms (learning rate modulation and freezing release probabilities) yields a noticeable decrease in performance during lifelong learning.
source: This yields a noticeable decrease in performance during lifelong learning, thus supporting the view that stabilising important synapses contributes to addressing the stability-plasticity dilemma.
evidence: This is supported by ablation study data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Presynaptic plasticity, on top of consolidation, helps to stabilise the network.
source: This suggests that presynaptic plasticity, on top of consolidation, helps to stabilise the network.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ablation study results.

claim: The sparsity induced by presynaptic plasticity decreases overlap between different tasks.
source: We believe that this can be attributed to the sparsity induced by the presynaptic plasticity which decreases overlap between different tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: The presynaptically consolidated perceptron maintains a more stable memory of the first task.
source: We find that the presynaptically consolidated perceptron maintains a more stable memory of the first task, see Figure 5b.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The effects of presynaptic consolidation extend beyond gradient-based learning.
source: and shows that the effects of presynaptic consolidation in our model extend beyond gradient-based learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the perceptron experiments.

claim: Presynaptic stochasticity enables networks to allocate energy more efficiently.
source: Introducing a simple model of the all-or-nothing nature of synaptic transmission, we show that presynaptic stochasticity enables networks to allocate energy more efficiently.
evidence: This is a main finding supported by the energy efficiency experiments.

claim: Learned release probabilities encode the importance of weights for network function according to the Fisher information.
source: We find theoretically as well as empirically that learned release probabilities encode the importance of weights for network function according to the Fisher information.
evidence: This is supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical data.

claim: Coupling information encoded in the release probabilities with modulated plasticity can help alleviate the stability-plasticity dilemma.
source: Our experiments provide evidence that coupling information encoded in the release probabilities with modulated plasticity can help alleviate the stability-plasticity dilemma.
evidence: This is supported by the lifelong learning experiments.

claim: The locus of expression for long-term plasticity can both be presynaptic and postsynaptic.
source: A central property of our model builds on the observation that the locus of expression for long-term plasticity can both be presynaptic and postsynaptic (Larkman et al., 1992; Lisman and Raghavachari, 2006; Bayazitov et al., 2007; Sjöström et al., 2007; Bliss and Collingridge, 2013; Costa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The mechanisms to change presynaptic and postsynaptic plasticity are distinct and synapse-specific.
source: The mechanisms to change either are distinct and synapse-specific (Yang and Calakos, 2013; Castillo, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang and Calakos, 2013 and Castillo, 2012.

claim: The induction of long-term plasticity is thought to be triggered postsynaptically for both presynaptic and postsynaptic changes.
source: The induction of long-term plasticity is thought to be triggered postsynaptically for both presynaptic and postsynaptic changes (Yang and Calakos, 2013; Padamsey and Emptage, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang and Calakos, 2013 and Padamsey and Emptage, 2014.

claim: Several forms of presynaptic plasticity require retrograde signalling.
source: and several forms of presynaptic plasticity are known to require retrograde signalling (Monday et al., 2018), for example through nitric oxide or endocannabinoids (Heifets and Castillo, 2009; Andrade-Talavera et al., 2016; Costa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: At least one form of presynaptic long-term plasticity is bidirectional switching from potentiation to depression depending on endocannabinoid transients.
source: At least one form of presynaptic long-term plasticity is known to be bidirectional switching from potentiation to depression depending on endocannabinoid transients (Cui et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2015 and Cui et al., 2016.

claim: Presynaptic boutons which contain stationary mitochondria are more stable than those which do not, both on short and long timescales of at least weeks.
source: Qualitatively, this is in line with observations that presynaptic boutons, which contain stationary mitochondria (Chang et al., 2006; Obashi and Okabe, 2013), are more stable than those which do not, both on short (Sun et al., 2013) and long timescales of at least weeks (Lees et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Synapses with higher initial release probability are more stable than those with low release probabilities for both LTP and LTD.
source: Appendix 1—figure 4 shows that synapses with higher initial release probability are more stable than those with low release probabilities for both LTP and LTD.
evidence: This is supported by re-analysis of data from Sjöström et al., 2001.

claim: Several alternatives to backpropagation aiming to increase biological plausibility exist and are compatible with the model.
source: Whether credit assignment in the brain relies on backpropagation – or more generally gradients – remains an active area of research, but several alternatives aiming to increase biological plausibility exist and are compatible with our model (Sacramento et al., 2018; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to alternative learning algorithms.

claim: Improved energy efficiency can at least partly be attributed to the sparsification induced by presynaptic stochasticity.
source: Our experiments suggest that improved energy efficiency can at least partly be attributed to the sparsification induced by presynaptic stochasticity (cf. Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: A wide range of sensory networks rely on sparse representations.
source: This includes a wide range of sensory networks (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Hahnloser et al., 2002; Crochet et al., 2011; Quiroga et al., 2005) as well as areas in the hippocampus (Wixted et al., 2014; Lodge and Bischofberger, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The introduced consolidation mechanism could benefit the slow part of a complementary learning system.
source: Generally, the introduced consolidation mechanism could benefit the slow part of a complementary learning system as proposed by McClelland et al., 1995; Kumaran et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a speculative connection to existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: Larger spines in the mouse barrel cortex are more stable.
source: Indeed, in line with the hypothesis that synapses with larger release probability are more stable, it has been observed that larger spines in the mouse barrel cortex are more stable.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Novel experiences lead to the formation of new, stable spines.
source: Moreover, novel experiences lead to the formation of new, stable spines, similar to our findings reported in Appendix 1—figure 3b.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and is consistent with the model's findings.

claim: Neural variability is often interpreted as representing uncertainty.
source: Inspired by a Bayesian perspective, neural variability is often interpreted as representing uncertainty (Ma et al., 2006; Fiser et al., 2010; Kappel et al., 2015; Haefner et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Neural variability is interpreted as a means to prevent overfitting.
source: neural variability is often interpreted as representing uncertainty (Ma et al., 2006; Fiser et al., 2010; Kappel et al., 2015; Haefner et al., 2016), or as a means to prevent overfitting (Wan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wan et al., 2013.

claim: The Bayesian paradigm has been applied directly to variability of individual synapses in neuroscience.
source: The Bayesian paradigm has been applied directly to variability of individual synapses in neuroscience (Aitchison et al., 2014; Aitchison and Latham, 2015; Aitchison et al., 2021) and machine learning (Zeno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant work.

claim: The Bayesian paradigm prescribes decreasing the plasticity of synapses with low posterior variance.
source: It prescribes decreasing the plasticity of synapses with low posterior variance.
evidence: This is based on Bayesian principles as applied in the cited work.

claim: Common Bayesian interpretations model release statistics as Gaussians and optimise complex objectives.
source: In contrast to common Bayesian interpretations (Zeno et al., 2018; Aitchison and Latham, 2015; Kappel et al., 2015) which model release statistics as Gaussians and optimise complex objectives (see also Llera-Montero et al., 2019)
evidence: This is based on the authors' review of Bayesian approaches in the literature.

claim: The proposed model represents the inherently discrete nature of synaptic transmission more faithfully than Bayesian models.
source: our simple proposal represents the inherently discrete nature of synaptic transmission more faithfully.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about the model's properties.

claim: The model's consolidation mechanism is similar to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC).
source: In the context of lifelong learning, our model's consolidation mechanism is similar to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), which explicitly relies on the Fisher information to consolidate synapses.
evidence: This is a comparison to existing methods.

claim: Unlike EWC, the proposed learning rule does not require a task switch signal and does not need a separate consolidation phase.
source: Unlike EWC, our learning rule does not require a task switch signal and does not need a separate consolidation phase.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about the model's properties.

claim: The model can be interpreted as using distinct states of plasticity to protect memories.
source: Moreover, our model can be interpreted as using distinct states of plasticity to protect memories. This general idea is formalised and analysed thoroughly by theoretical work on cascade models of plasticity (Fusi et al., 2005; Roxin and Fusi, 2013; Benna and Fusi, 2016).
evidence: This is a conceptual connection to existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: The cascade model has been shown to be effective in lifelong learning settings.
source: The resulting model (Benna and Fusi, 2016) has also been shown to be effective in lifelong learning settings (Kaplanis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benna and Fusi, 2016 and Kaplanis et al., 2018.

claim: Energy constraints are widely believed to be a main driver of evolution.
source: Energy constraints are widely believed to be a main driver of evolution (Niven and Laughlin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niven and Laughlin, 2008.

claim: Brain size has been shown to be optimal in terms of metabolic cost.
source: From brain size (Isler and van Schaik, 2009; Navarrete et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on brain size.

claim: Wiring cost has been shown to be optimal in terms of metabolic cost.
source: to wiring cost (Chen et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2006.

claim: Ion channel properties have been shown to be optimal in terms of metabolic cost.
source: down to ion channel properties (Alle et al., 2009; Sengupta et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on ion channels.

claim: Presynaptic transmitter release has been shown to be optimal in terms of metabolic cost.
source: presynaptic transmitter release (Savtchenko et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Savtchenko et al., 2013.

claim: Postsynaptic conductance has been shown to be optimal in terms of metabolic cost.
source: and postsynaptic conductance (Harris et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2015.

claim: The central nervous system operates in varying regimes, making different trade-offs between synaptic energy demand and information transmission.
source: Crucially, there is evidence that the central nervous system operates in varying regimes, making different trade-offs between synaptic energy demand and information transmission: Perge et al., 2009; Carter and Bean, 2009; Hu and Jonas, 2014 all find properties of the axon (thickness, sodium channel properties), which are suboptimal in terms of energy per bit of information.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Inefficiencies in axon properties occur to ensure fast transmission of highly relevant information.
source: They suggest that these inefficiencies occur to ensure fast transmission of highly relevant information.
evidence: This is an interpretation from the cited studies.

claim: A similar energy/information trade-off could govern network dynamics preferentially allocating more energy to the most relevant synapses for a given task.
source: We propose that a similar energy/information trade-off could govern network dynamics preferentially allocating more energy to the most relevant synapses for a given task.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the model's findings.

claim: The proposed trade-off and overall energy savings cannot be accounted for by previous frameworks for energy-efficient information transmission at synapses.
source: Neither the trade-off nor the overall savings can be accounted for by previous frameworks for energy-efficient information transmission at synapses (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Release probabilities and related metabolic cost provide a way to make the informal notion of 'synaptic importance' concrete by measuring how much energy is spent on a synapse.
source: This view of release probabilities and related metabolic cost provides a way to make the informal notion of 'synaptic importance' concrete by measuring how much energy is spent on a synapse.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's findings.

claim: The notion of synaptic importance is helpful beyond purely energetic considerations and can help to maintain memories during lifelong learning.
source: Interestingly, our model suggests that this notion is helpful beyond purely energetic considerations and can in fact help to maintain memories during lifelong learning.
evidence: This is supported by the lifelong learning experiments.

claim: The main constituent of neural energy demand is synaptic signal transmission.
source: Harris et al., 2012 find that the main constituent of neural energy demand is synaptic signal transmission
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The cost of synaptic signal transmission is dominated by the energy needed to reverse postsynaptic ion fluxes.
source: and that the cost of synaptic signal transmission is dominated by the energy needed to reverse postsynaptic ion fluxes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The Fisher information is a measure for the networks sensitivity to changes in parameters.
source: The Fisher information is a measure for the networks sensitivity to changes in parameters.
evidence: This is based on established mathematical theory.

claim: Under additional assumptions the Fisher information is equal to the Hessian of the loss function.
source: Under additional assumptions it is equal to the Hessian of the loss function (Pascanu and Bengio, 2013; Martens, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pascanu and Bengio, 2013 and Martens, 2014.

claim: The Fisher information equals the Hessian of the cross entropy loss with respect to the model parameters under the assumption that the learned probability distribution equals the real probability distribution.
source: Under the assumption that the learned probability distribution f(⋅∣X,θ) equals the real probability distribution, the Fisher information equals the Hessian of the cross entropy loss (i.e. the negative log-probabilities) with respect to the model parameters (Pascanu and Bengio, 2013; Martens, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The Fisher information was previously used in machine learning to enable lifelong learning.
source: The Fisher information was previously used in machine learning to enable lifelong learning (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Huszár, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Other popular lifelong learning methods implicitly rely on the Fisher information.
source: and it has been shown that other popular lifelong learning methods implicitly rely on the Fisher information (Benzing, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benzing, 2020.
